summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct between adults is not criminalised in the Republic of the Congo. A systematic review of the country's legislation carried out for the European Union Agency for Asylum's May 2024 country-of-origin information query found no law prohibiting such conduct, and the United States State Department's 2022 and 2023 human rights reports state that no statute specifically bans it. Those reports record no arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons on the basis of same-sex conduct during 2023.

The Penal Code does draw a line at Article 331, which sets the age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts against 18 for different-sex acts and punishes "shameless acts or acts against nature" with a person of the same sex under the age of 21 by six months to three years' imprisonment and a fine. The scope of that provision as applied to same-sex conduct is described as ambiguous in the sources cited by the EUAA response, which also reports that it is treated as a basis for discriminatory treatment. The United States State Department records that the provision was not invoked to bring prosecutions in 2022 or 2023.

Police have nevertheless used the provision as a pretext to solicit bribes from gay men, and the practice is documented in both the 2022 and the 2023 reporting, which places the immediate legal exposure for an LGBTQI+ person in the hands of officers rather than in a courtroom. Local organisations reported to the same reporting that LGBTQI+ persons face violence, psychological and physical harassment and financial extortion at the hands of both government actors and non-state actors, continuing through 2023.

The statute offers no anti-discrimination protection of any kind. Nothing in the reviewed legislation provides a remedy for the extortion and harassment documented by the local organisations, and the EUAA response records the availability of state protection as a matter examined in its own right rather than as a settled guarantee.
tangentialFactors:
The under-21 provision has not lain idle: its utility to police as a lever for extracting bribes from gay men is recorded in two consecutive years of reporting, so a visitor's most likely encounter with it is an demand for money during a stop, search or questioning rather than a charge. That distinction matters when weighing whether the absence of prosecutions indicates safety.

The divergence between the age of consent for same-sex acts and for different-sex acts signals a legal framework that distinguishes same-sex conduct in the statute book even where it does not prohibit it outright, and sources cited in the EUAA response treat the same provision as a footing for discriminatory treatment by officials and private parties alike.

Reported abuse is attributable to state and non-state actors in roughly equal measure, which complicates any assumption that the risk is confined to official encounters or, conversely, to street crime. Violence, psychological harassment and financial extortion are all named.

The regime bears comparison with jurisdictions where consensual conduct is lawful yet no protective statute exists: the Republic of the Congo combines non-criminalisation with the complete absence of anti-discrimination protection, leaving recourse dependent on the willingness of police rather than on an enforceable right.
localsOnly:
Residents living under Article 331 face an age of consent fixed at 21 for same-sex acts while different-sex acts are governed by the age of 18, a disparity that shapes the exposure of same-sex couples well into adulthood and leaves the under-21 provision available to officers as an discretionary tool.

Local organisations report that LGBTQI+ people in the country endure violence, psychological and physical harassment and financial extortion from both government and non-state actors, with the pattern reported as continuing into 2023.

No anti-discrimination protection exists in law, so persons subjected to the extortion and harassment documented by those organisations have no statutory claim to invoke. Police use of the "act against nature" language to solicit bribes from gay men is a reported feature of routine contact rather than an exceptional event.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any completed prosecution under the under-21 provision has ever occurred is not established in the sources reviewed here; the available reporting states only that it has not been invoked in 2022 or 2023.

The inventory records that the EUAA response examined implementation, treatment by state and society, and the availability of state protection for LGBTQI+ people, but it does not carry a specific finding on state protection requests, and none is asserted here.

No sourced material was supplied on legal gender recognition, the rules governing gender markers on passports or other travel documents, restroom or facility access, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, marriage or partner recognition, military service, blood donation, or immigration and entry screening as it affects trans travellers. Whether such screening occurs at Brazzaville or Pointe-Noire ports of entry remains unresolved.

The nationality and mandate of the local organisations reporting the harassment and extortion are not identified in the inventory, and neither is the disposition of any complaint they may have filed.
